metaDescription: Three Midea countertop dishwashers compared: a 6-setting Energy Star faucet unit and two tank models with turbofan or dual drying, plus cabinet clearance tips.
expertTake: The six-setting Energy Star Midea is the best overall because it holds the most and runs from the faucet. The auto-open tank model is the pick for renters. Anyone short of clearance under a wall cabinet should skip the tank model with its 20.8 inch requirement.
introParagraphs: A small lineup of countertop washers from one maker can split cleanly into two designs. One connects to the faucet and holds a proper six place settings. The others fill from a built-in tank and focus on drying and baby care, which changes how they fit a kitchen.

Because each design asks for different clearance, plumbing and habits, the useful question is not which one is best in the abstract. It is which one fits your counter height, your faucet and the dishes you actually wash.

products.description:
The faucet-fed Midea is the one that behaves most like a small full-size dishwasher. It holds six place settings, enough for two or three people according to the maker, and carries an Energy Star rating with a 52 dB noise level. A hose connects to the faucet with a suitable adaptor, so the machine never runs short of water mid-cycle.

Its cycle list is the broadest of the three: Auto, Heavy, Normal, Quick, Rinse and Delicate, plus Extended Dry and Power Wash functions as add-ons. Auto adjusts the wash to how dirty the load is, which saves a new owner from choosing. Against the two tank models it gives up placement freedom, since it needs a faucet, and it is the largest body at 17.25 inches high, 22 inches wide and 20 inches deep.

The size is the thing to plan around. A 22 inch width eats a lot of counter, and the faucet adaptor is not a given. Check that your spout accepts the standard thread before ordering. After that it is a low-effort machine: attach the hose, load, run and drain. Rinse the filter regularly and leave the door cracked afterward.
products.bestFor: Two or three people with a threaded faucet and a generous counter.
pros: Six place settings with an Energy Star rating
Auto cycle picks the wash level for you
Extended Dry and Power Wash add-on functions
Faucet feed removes the tank refill chore
cons: Largest body at 22 inches wide and 20 inches deep
Needs a faucet adaptor that many kitchens lack

products.name: Midea Countertop Dishwasher, 1.59 Gal Tank, Auto-Open Door, Turbofan

specList.label: Clearance
specList.value: More than 20.8 in under the cabinet

products.description:
This tank model is built around drying. At the end of each cycle the door opens by itself and a built-in turbofan pushes air through the chamber, which tackles the stale, damp finish that dogs most small washers. A 1.59 gallon tank, about 6 liters, feeds five programs: Normal, Rapid, Hygiene, Fruit and Glass, with two additional functions.

The auto-open door is clever and has a catch: the listing asks that the distance between your countertop and wall cupboard be more than 20.8 inches. A door that swings upward needs that headroom, and a low cabinet will block it. Compared with the 1.32 gallon Midea below it holds a quarter more water and adds the fan, but it asks for more vertical room.

For ownership, the self-opening door removes the habit of propping it, though you should still empty the tank when the machine sits for days. Clean the filter every few loads, and measure the cabinet gap before ordering. It suits renters who want a no-hookup machine that dries well. Dry plates matter more than owners expect, because damp dishes stacked in a cupboard grow odor within a day. The turbofan also helps the machine itself, since a chamber that dries fully is far less likely to develop a musty smell.
products.bestFor: Renters and small-kitchen owners who want strong drying without a faucet.
pros: Door opens automatically at the end of each cycle
1.59 gallon tank, larger than the other tank Midea
cons: Needs more than 20.8 inches under the wall cabinet

products.name: Midea Countertop Dishwasher, 1.32 Gal Tank, Baby Care, 5+1 Programs

specList.label: Programs
specList.value: Baby Care, Delicate, Normal, Quick, Fruit

products.description:
The second tank model targets families with babies. Its program list is Baby Care, Delicate, Normal, Quick and Fruit, plus one extra function, and the maker describes an improved cleaning power for the Baby Care cycle. A dual drying system combines high-temperature drying with residual-heat drying, which dries bottles and small parts more thoroughly than relying on leftover heat alone.

The tank holds 1.32 gallons, about 5 liters, a little less than the 1.59 gallon Midea, and the machine needs no hookup. It lacks the auto-open door and turbofan of its sibling, but it keeps a lower profile and probably fits under more cabinets because the listing does not repeat the 20.8 inch requirement. Against the faucet-fed unit it trades capacity for flexibility.

Use it for bottles, pacifiers, small plates and cups. Check the manual on which plastics tolerate the high-temperature cycle, and empty the tank after use. A quick filter rinse every few loads keeps small parts from carrying residue. Place nipples, valves and small caps in a closed basket so they do not drop into the chamber and block a spray arm. Parents often run this machine twice a day, so the filter matters more here than in a lightly used kitchen.
products.bestFor: New parents washing bottles and small plates every day.
pros: Baby Care program tuned for bottles and small parts
Dual drying combines high heat with residual heat
cons: Smaller tank than the 1.59 gallon Midea
Small chamber suits light loads only

buyingCriteria.explanation: Midea splits its countertop line into a faucet-fed six-setting machine and two tank-fed models. The faucet unit never runs out of water and has the biggest chamber, but it needs a threaded faucet and sits beside the sink. The tank models go anywhere and need a refill every load. Decide the supply question before you compare anything else, because it settles the shortlist in most kitchens. A quick check is to unscrew the faucet aerator and look for threads on the spout. If you find none, or you rent and cannot change the spout, the tank models are the realistic choice, whatever the capacity gap looks like on paper.

Dimensions decide fit. The faucet model is 17.25 inches high, 22 inches wide and 20 inches deep. The auto-open tank model asks for more than 20.8 inches between the counter and the wall cupboard so the door can lift. Measure vertical gaps with a tape, not by eye. A machine that cannot open fully is a machine you will not use. Also measure the width of the space you intend to use, because a 22 inch body leaves little room for a kettle or toaster beside it. Leave a few inches behind for the hose and the steam vent, and do not park it beneath a shelf that traps hot air.

Drying is the weak point of countertop washers. The 1.59 gallon Midea opens its door and runs a turbofan, and the 1.32 gallon Midea combines high-temperature and residual drying. The faucet model offers an Extended Dry function. Each approach helps, but none matches a vented full-size machine. Prop the door and towel-dry plastics in any case. Plastic holds heat poorly, so containers and baby gear come out wet even after a hot cycle. Place them on the top rack tilted so water runs off, and let them air-dry on a clean towel, not stacked inside a cupboard.

The faucet-fed Midea quotes 52 dB, which is moderate rather than quiet. Tank minis from other makers claim 40 dB, so in a studio apartment it is worth comparing. Noise depends heavily on how level the counter is and what is underneath the machine. A thin mat under the feet cuts rattle. Stone counters amplify vibration, and an uneven surface makes the machine walk during the spin phase. If the noise annoys you, move the load to a time you are out of the room, using a timer function if the model has one.

The faucet unit has an Auto cycle that senses soil level, plus Heavy, Normal, Quick, Rinse and Delicate. The tank models have Normal, Rapid, Hygiene, Fruit and Glass or Baby Care, Delicate, Normal, Quick and Fruit. Match the list to your dishes: Baby Care for bottles, Glass for stemware, Auto for mixed loads. A program you never use is wasted space on the dial. The tank models in particular rely on Hygiene or Baby Care for hot washes, so check which plastics the maker says can take that heat. When in doubt, run a gentler program and rely on a good pre-rinse.

Only the faucet model states place settings, at six. The tank models give a tank volume and little else, so treat them as one or two person machines. A six-setting machine holds about a full dinner for three, while a tank model holds a day of cups and plates for two. Match the capacity to your household before you match features. Overfilling any of them is the most common cause of dirty results, since plates shadow each other from the spray. Leave gaps between items, and run a second small load instead of cramming one big one.

howWeEvaluated.title: Water supply and placement
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the faucet unit with the two tank models for flexibility and convenience. The faucet unit wins for hands-off use, and the tank models win for placement freedom. We did not treat either as superior in general.

howWeEvaluated.title: Clearance and fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We used the 22 inch width and 20 inch depth of the faucet unit and the 20.8 inch headroom of the auto-open model as the key fit numbers. A machine that fits a wider range of kitchens scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drying
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the drying features: Extended Dry on the faucet unit, turbofan with auto-open on the 1.59 gallon model and dual drying on the baby care model. The turbofan model scored highest for actually clearing moisture.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cycle usefulness
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at whether programs map to real jobs. Auto, Baby Care and Glass earned credit. Overlapping Quick and Rapid modes earned little.

howWeEvaluated.title: Efficiency and noise
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted the Energy Star rating and the 52 dB figure on the faucet model as concrete claims. The tank models state neither in the available text. This is based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns. Where a figure was missing we said so and avoided guessing, since a silent gap in a listing is not the same as a poor result. Readers should check the manual for anything the listing leaves out.

cards.label: Faucet unit
cards.text: The Energy Star Midea holds six place settings and never runs short of water. It is wide and deep, and it needs a faucet adaptor that may not fit.

cards.label: Tank unit
cards.text: The two tank Mideas fill by hand and sit anywhere. They hold less, and the 1.59 gallon model needs extra headroom for its door.

howToChoose.note: Choose the faucet unit for capacity, and a tank unit for placement and renters. The Auto cycle on the faucet unit is worth trying first on mixed loads, since it adjusts the wash to the soil it senses, and Heavy suits baked-on pans while Delicate suits glassware. Tank owners should plan to refill before each load and to empty the tank after it.

maintenance.why: Debris clogs the screen and weakens spray. Baby bottle residue is especially quick to build. Twist the filter out, rinse it under running water and brush off any film before you seat it again.
Tank models only. Standing water breeds odor even with a fan-assisted chamber. Dry the tank with a cloth, and leave its cap off so air can circulate until the next load.
Residue spreads odor, and a gritty gasket stops the door from sealing. Run a fingertip along the lip to feel for grit, and wipe the area under the latch where food film collects.
Use dishwasher cleaner to dissolve grease and scale. Never use hand soap.
Faucet model only. A worn washer leaks into the cabinet before you see a puddle.

faq.q: Which Midea has the most capacity?
faq.a: The faucet-fed Energy Star model, with six place settings and a body of 22 by 20 inches. The tank models list volumes instead of settings. In practice, expect the tank models to hold a day of cups, bowls and small plates for one or two people, and plan on a second cycle when guests visit.

faq.q: Does the auto-open door need extra space?
faq.a: Yes, and it is worth measuring before you buy. The 1.59 gallon model asks for more than 20.8 inches between the countertop and the wall cupboard so the door can open. If your cabinets sit lower, the 1.32 gallon model, which does not list that requirement, or the faucet unit are the better candidates. Measure from the counter surface to the underside of the cabinet, not to the wall.

The listings we evaluated do not state a noise figure. The faucet unit quotes 52 dB, so compare that against your own tolerance. A fan-assisted drying phase on the 1.59 gallon model adds its own whir at the end of a cycle, so run any of them while you are out of the room if sound bothers you.

faq.q: Is Baby Care different from Hygiene?
faq.a: Both use higher heat. Baby Care is tuned to bottles and small parts, while Hygiene is a general hot cycle. Check the manual for plastic limits. Neither replaces sterilizing guidance from a pediatrician, so treat them as a convenient hot wash and not as a medical step.

faq.q: Can I connect a tank model to the faucet?
faq.a: The listings describe the tank models as no-hookup units. Only the Energy Star model is described as faucet-fed. That distinction matters more than any cycle name, because a machine you cannot connect is a machine you cannot use. Renters who cannot modify a faucet should therefore treat the Energy Star model as off the table and shop between the two tank units, using the baby care and drying differences to decide.

With clean filters and a dry chamber, small pumps and heaters last for years. Neglect is the usual cause of early failure. Scale from hard water is the second slow killer, so descale the chamber with a dishwasher cleaner every month or two if your tap water leaves white film on glass.
